findings.category: cfunc exception-swallow / silent output corruption at the C boundary
findings.title: Scalar-UDF @cfunc callbacks have no exception guard; a raise inside the impl is swallowed at numba's cfunc boundary, handing DuckDB a silent 'success' with a partially-written/garbage output vector and no error signalled
findings.description: Both scalar chunk callbacks are thin @cfunc wrappers over a module-level @njit impl with no try/except: _haversine_chunk_cb (haversine.py:116-118) -> _haversine_chunk_impl (haversine.py:87-113), and _fraud_chunk_cb (fraud_score.py:147-149) -> _fraud_chunk_impl (fraud_score.py:102-144). Per the codebase's verified numba contract (MEMORY reference_numba_cfunc_swallows_exceptions; confirmed against numba's np_cfarray) a Python exception escaping an impl called from a @cfunc is caught at the boundary, printed to stderr, and the void zero-default is returned WITHOUT unwinding into DuckDB. DuckDB therefore treats the scalar callback as successful and consumes whatever values were already written into the output vector (a_out, written in place at haversine.py:113 / fraud_score.py:144) up to the raise point -- a silent wrong result for the whole chunk with no SQL-level error. IMPORTANT DISTINCTION FROM THE UDAF FINDING (XC-numbox-MEM-1 / EX-irr-MEM-1): the scalar impls hold NO NRT reference across any call, so the swallow's leak component does NOT apply here. Every carray view is created unmanaged -- numba's np_cfarray calls populate_array(..., meminfo=None, '# Array is not memory-managed') (arrayobj.py:5574-5581) -- and _cast_int_to_void_p is a pure inttoptr with no incref (numbox lowlevel.py:49-53); the impls never take a borrow_structref/export_meminfo +1 (contrast irr.py). So there is nothing to leak: the sole consequence is the silent corrupt/partial output. Reachability is latent: for the examples' own dense non-NULL numeric inputs no impl actually raises (numba's math.sqrt/asin return NaN on domain errors rather than raising; the loops use only float/int comparisons, adds, and in-bounds carray writes; n comes from duckdb_data_chunk_get_size and carray does not validate the backing buffer), so a raise is reachable only via a future edit that introduces a raising call, or a port to nullable/validity-checked inputs.
findings.impact: If either impl ever raises (future edit adds a raising call, or the pattern is copied to nullable inputs), DuckDB silently returns a wrong scalar result for the entire chunk -- the output vector holds whatever was computed before the raise (garbage for the un-reached rows) and no error reaches SQL. No memory is leaked (carray views are unmanaged, meminfo=None). As the two canonical scalar-UDF usage examples, they teach an idiom with no swallow guard, so the corruption becomes live the moment a raising operation is added.
findings.recommendation: For parity with the numbox phase-3 UDAF guard and XC-numbox-MEM-1, either wrap each impl body in a bare try/except (NOT try/finally -- it re-raises on numba 0.65.1) that writes a defined sentinel to the output on failure, or, since the current binding set exposes no per-row error-signalling channel for a chunk scalar callback, at minimum add a comment at each @cfunc wrapper documenting the swallow-on-raise contract and the invariant that the impl must stay raise-free, so a future edit does not silently introduce an uncaught raising call.

notes: Full MEM audit of both scalar examples against the numbox meminfo/lowlevel contract and DuckDB's scalar-callback vector ownership. HAPPY-PATH LIFETIME / BOUNDS / REFCOUNT MODEL IS SOUND: (1) carray views (fraud_score.py:118-124, haversine.py:99-103) alias DuckDB-owned vector buffers only for the duration of the callback, during which DuckDB owns the chunk and its vectors; no view outlives the callback, so no use-after-free. They are unmanaged (numba np_cfarray -> populate_array meminfo=None, arrayobj.py:5574-5581) so they neither own nor free the DuckDB buffers and cannot leak NRT. (2) OUTPUT-WRITE BOUNDS SAFE: n = duckdb_data_chunk_get_size(chunk) is <= STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE (2048); the scalar output vector DuckDB passes is a flat buffer of capacity STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE; a_out is written only over [0,n) (haversine.py:113, fraud_score.py:144). (3) HANDLE-DESTROY CORRECT ON THE HAPPY PATH: logical types are created once and destroyed exactly once even though reused for multiple params (fraud_score.py:166-168 loops the 3 distinct types dbl/tin/int; haversine.py:131-132 destroys the single reused DOUBLE once) -- safe because DuckDB copies the type on add_parameter/set_return_type; the destroy-by-buffer idiom keeps the numpy handle buffer alive across the C call (it is a named local: func_buf/type_buf/buf), and the scalar-function handle is destroyed once after register (fraud_score.py:172-173, haversine.py:136-137). No double-free. (4) The @cfunc objects are module-level globals (fraud_score.py:147, haversine.py:116) so the raw function pointer handed to DuckDB via .address outlives registration and every query -- no dangling callback. CROSS-REFERENCES to already-filed defects that also bear on MEM (deliberately NOT re-filed here, to avoid duplicate findings): (a) EX-hav-1 (filed COR, high) -- haversine calls hv_jit(lat, lon, 37.7749, -122.4194) with SQL literal constants as args 2,3; if DuckDB delivers a BoundConstantExpression as a CONSTANT_VECTOR (1-element data buffer) the kernel's a_lat2[i]/a_lon2[i] for i>=1 (haversine.py:101-102 carray shaped (n,), read at 107-112) is a heap over-read of up to ~2047 doubles past an 8-byte buffer -- the dominant MEM-relevant defect in the scalar examples. fraud_score is NOT exposed to this because all six of its arguments are table columns (flat vectors of size n), not literals. (b) EX-fraud-1 / EX-hav-2 (filed COR) -- the builder handle func_p leaks on the register-failure path because 'assert rc == DuckDBSuccess' (fraud_score.py:171, haversine.py:135) precedes the destroy (fraud_score.py:172-173, haversine.py:136-137); process-fatal here so negligible in practice, but an unsafe idiom to copy. NET: the only NEW MEM finding is EX-scalar-MEM-1 (the scalar-path analog of the UDAF cfunc-swallow finding, but strictly weaker: no NRT reference is held across a call so nothing leaks, and no impl reachably raises for the examples' inputs -- a latent robustness gap, not a live memory bug).
